questions.q: In Salesforce Field Service, which object represents the job itself, as distinct from a specific scheduled visit?
options: Work Order
Service Resource
Scheduling Policy
Service Objective
questions.explain: The Work Order represents the job to be done. A Service Appointment is the specific scheduled visit tied to that Work Order, and a Service Resource is the technician who might be assigned to it — three distinct objects, not one.

questions.q: A technician lacks the certification required for a commercial chiller repair. How does a scheduling policy's work rule handle this, as opposed to a service objective?
options: It lowers the technician's score but still allows them to be selected if no one else is available
It removes the technician from consideration entirely as a hard filter, rather than scoring them lower
Work rules only apply to Service Appointments, never to technician qualifications
It automatically trains the technician before assignment
questions.explain: Work rules are hard filters: a candidate that fails one is removed from consideration outright. Service objectives are the soft, weighted scoring criteria applied only to the candidates who survive the hard filters.

questions.q: Castellan's emergency no-heat calls keep losing out to geographically convenient routine jobs. What kind of fix does this lesson say the problem calls for?
options: A new work rule banning routine maintenance Work Orders entirely
Removing all Service Resources from the routine maintenance queue
A scheduling policy that weights the priority service objective more heavily relative to travel-time efficiency, such as a separate Emergency policy
Disabling the Dispatcher Console's Gantt view
questions.explain: This is a weighting problem among soft service objectives (priority vs. travel-time efficiency), not a hard-filter problem — the fix is a scheduling policy, potentially a separate Emergency policy, that weights urgency heavily enough to beat out travel-time convenience.

questions.q: What does this lesson say nothing in Castellan's original whiteboard process was actually tracking, which is why double-booking happened?
options: The customer's billing address
The Work Order's priority field
The technician's hourly pay rate
Each resource's calendar as its own object, independent from "the job" as one undifferentiated concept
questions.explain: The whiteboard process conflated the job, the scheduled visit, and the technician's calendar into one mental model, so nothing enforced that a single resource's calendar couldn't hold two overlapping appointments — exactly what Service Appointments tied to Service Resources are built to prevent.

questions.q: When a dispatcher manually drags an appointment onto a technician who violates a configured work rule, what does Field Service's Dispatcher Console do?
options: It warns the dispatcher about the violation but does not block the override outright
It silently applies the change with no indication anything is wrong
It permanently locks the dispatcher out of making manual changes
It automatically reassigns the appointment to a different technician without asking
questions.explain: The design explicitly allows dispatcher override using local knowledge the system doesn't have, but warns when a manual change violates a configured work rule — which is why it matters that every rule worth warning about is actually configured as a work rule in the first place.
